OPP 20.
Both the issues were inter-related and hence, they were taken together.
The plaintiff has stated to be in possession of the suit property.
However, it has not been stated specifically as to what portion of the suit property has been occupied by him.
The case of the plaintiff is that defendants No.1 and defendant No.2 have raised unauthorized construction on the suit property which has caused damage to the portion of the plaintiff.

The case set up by the plaintiff is that he was adopted by late Sardar Jasbir Singh i.e. son of late Sardar Jodh Singh, when he was only three years old and since then he is residing in the suit property.
It is the case of the plaintiff that though the suit property was purchased in the name of Mrs. Harbhajan Kaur but the same was purchased by the funds of late Sardar Jodh Singh.
It is the further case of the plaintiff that on the death of late Sardar Jodh Singh, he also become co-owner of the suit property along with defendant No.1 and defendant No.2.

It is pleaded by the plaintiff that the defendant No.1 has prepared a false GPA purportedly executed by Mrs. Harbhajan Kaur in his favour and on the strength of this GPA, he executed a false gift deed in favour of his wife.
The title of the plaintiff has been disputed by the defendants.

Admittedly, the parties have filed suits against each other i.e. suit for partition and declaration filed by the plaintiff against defendants, and suit for possession and injunction filed by wife of defendant No.1 against the plaintiff.
During the pendency of these case, the present suit was filed.
21. It is an admitted fact that title of the plaintiff has been disputed by the defendants.
The plaintiff himself has described about the circumstances which suggests ouster of the plaintiff from the suit property.
The plaintiff himself has stated about the execution of GPA and gift deed vesting the suit property in favour of wife of defendant No.1.
Therefore, it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to first prove his title to the suit property.
The suit for injunction simplicitor would not be maintainable unless the plaintiff has proven his title to the suit property.

In The Tehsildar, Urban Improvement Trust & Anr. Vs. Ganga Bai Menariya (Dead) Through Lrs. & Ors., 2024 2 SCR 650, it was observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court:
"21.

sentences.text: In the light of the aforesaid stand and the evidence led on record by the appellants-defendants, it was incumbent on the respondents to have proved their title on the land, which they failed to establish.
As per the stand of the appellants, the respondents were encroachers upon the land for which notice under Section 92A of the 1959 Act was issued to them.
The same was replied to by the respondents stating therein that they have patta executed in their favour by the Gram Panchayat.
21.1 Further a suit simpliciter for injunction may not be maintainable as the title of the property of the plaintiff/respondent was disputed by the appellants/defendants.
In such a situation it was required for the respondent/plaintiff to prove the title of the property while praying for injunction.
Reference can be made to the judgment of this Court in Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (Dead) by Lrs. and ors."

sentences.text: It is pertinent to mention that though the suit filed by the wife of defendant No.1 against the plaintiff for possession and injunction has been dismissed vide judgment dated 19.11.2022 in CS DJ No. 616986/2016, but there is no adjudication about the title of the plaintiff in the said suit.

Further,
the suit filed by the plaintiff seeking declaration against the GPA as well as gift deed and for partition, is still sub-judice.
As such there is no adjudication till date in favour of the plaintiff establishing his title to the suit property.
In the present suit also, the plaintiff has not led any evidence to establish his title to the suit property.

The following facts pleaded by the plaintiff has remained unsubstantiated during the trial:
(i) that the plaintiff was adopted by late Sardar Jodh Singh and Mrs. Harbhajan Kaur,
(ii) that the title of the suit property was held by Mrs. Harbhajan Kaur as a benami only and that after death of late Sardar Jodh Singh, the plaintiff also become co-owner of the suit property by succession,
(iii) that there was a family settlement arrived at between all the surviving heirs of late Sardar Jodh Singh in regard to the suit property,
(iv) that the plaintiff is enjoying the suit property as co- owner of the same.
In fact, no evidence was led by the plaintiff to prove the above facts.
It is submitted on behalf of the plaintiff that the plaintiff's right to possession can be inferred from will dated 20.10.2003 referred to in the judgment dated 19.11.2022.
However, no such will has been pleaded by the plaintiff in the present case nor the same was proved in accordance with the provisions of section 68 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
Hence, the claim of the plaintiff that he was co-owner of suit property and therefore, entitled to sue for injunction, has remained unproven.

As a consequence, it is to be concluded that the plaintiff was not entitled for the relief of injunction, be it perpetual or mandatory.

24. In Rajendra Motwani & Anr. Vs. MCD & Ors., RSA No. 243/2017, dated 16.10.2017, it was held that to sue for injunction complaining about unauthorized constructed, it is necessary to plead and prove that legal right of the plaintiff is infringed or that his easement right has been affected.

entities.text: Rajendra Motwani & Anr. Vs. MCD & Ors., RSA No. 243/2017
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was also held that in case of easementary right, it is necessary to plead and establish that the easement has been enjoyed for a continuous period of 20 years.

The relevant observations of the judgment read as under:
"8.
The second reason for rejecting the argument urged on behalf of the appellants/plaintiffs is that an illegal construction in itself does not give any legal right to a neighbor.

An illegal construction always no doubt gives locus standi to the local municipal authorities to seek removal of the illegal construction, but, a right of a neighbor only arises if the legal rights of light and air or any other legal right is affected by virtue of the illegal construction of the neighbor.

Legal right to light and air is only in terms of Section 15 of the Easements Act, 1882 which requires a cause of action to be laid out and proved that right to light and air has been enjoyed for 20 years and only on completion of 20 years there is a right to acquisition by prescription in the easementary rights.

It is relevant to note that even after acquisition of easementary rights of prescription, yet, right to injunction for a neighbor is not absolute and is covered by Section 33 of the Easements Act which requires that disturbance to the easementary rights must actually cause substantial damage to a neighbor and the infraction materially diminishes the value of the dominant heritage with the fact that there is material interference in the physical comfort of the neighbor of living in his own house or prevents the neighbor from carrying on his accustomed business in the dominant heritage/his own house.

All these are factual aspects and admittedly there is no cause of action which is laid out in the plaint in terms of Sections 15 and 33 of the Easements Act that right to easement of the appellants/plaintiffs has become absolute as it has been enjoyed for 20 years and that in fact after rights to easement are acquired by prescription there is also a substantial damage to the appellants/plaintiffs or there is material interference in the physical comfort of the appellants/plaintiffs or the appellants/plaintiffs being prevented from carrying on his accustomed business in their own dominant heritage/own property."

25. Similarly, It was held in C. Lal & Sons Vs Wasudhir Foundation, 1997 41 DRJ 327, that it is necessary for the plaintiff to prove before claiming injunction that he has personal interest in the subject matter of the suit and if he fails to do so, the suit would be hit by section 41 (j) of Specific Relief Act, 1963.

26. Moreover, the alleged unauthorized construction raised by the defendants was already complete when the present suit was filed.
There are no pleadings in regard to any threat or likelihood of a fresh construction in the suit property.
Therefore, in any event, there was no breach or attempt of breach of any obligation which would have warranted the suit for permanent injunction in the first place.
27. To summarize, the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit property and that his portion has suffered damage or his right to fresh air and light has been restricted.
Hence, the plaintiff is not entitled for any relief of injunction in respect of the suit property against the defendants.
In view of the above, issues No.1 and 2 are decided against the plaintiff and against the defendants.
Issue No.3
Whether the suit of the plaintiff is barred by the provisions of Section 477/478 of the DMC Act for want of statutory notice? OPD-3 28.
It is the preliminary objection taken by defendant No.3/MCD that the suit is not maintainable as no statutory notice was served upon it in terms of section 478 of DMC Act, 1957.
It is pertinent to mention that the provision itself provides an exception for the suits of injunction.

Moreover, the basic object of sections 477 and 478 of DMC Act is to prevent matters from coming to court and once the matter has reached the court and is contested, the suit ought not be dismissed on technical grounds.
In this regard, reliance can be had to the judgment of Col. A. B. Singh (through LRs) v. Shri Chunnilal Sawhney and Others, 2011 SCC OnLine Del 4289.

entities.text: Col. A. B. Singh (through LRs) v. Shri Chunnilal Sawhney and Others, 2011 SCC OnLine Del 4289
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, once defendant No.3/MCD has contested the present suit, it cannot be dismissed by recourse to section 477 and 478 of DMC Act.
Therefore, issue No.3 is decided against the defendant No.3 and in favour of the plaintiff.

opennyai_summary.facts:
This is a suit for permanent and mandatory injunction filed by the plaintiff against the defendants.
That late Mrs. Harbhajan Kaur was not having any source of income and she was a house wife through out her life and totally dependent on her husband financially and for her livelihood.
That during the life time of late Sardar Jasbir Singh, the plaintiff was adopted as son by late Sardar Jasbir Singh and his wife Mrs Harinder Luthra when the plaintiff was three days old.
That therefore by virtue of succession the plaintiff has equal right in the suit property.
That defendant No. 2 has raised the walls of his portion which has resulted in restraining the direct sunlight and fresh air in the house of the plaintiff and illegally and unlawfully constructed rooms at ground floor.
That moreover, defendant No.2 has raised walls in the common area.
That defendant No. 2 has no exclusive right to raise wall in the said part of the property.
That both defendants No. 1 and 2 have not obtained any permission from defendant No. 3 for raising construction in property.
That the plaintiff has met both the defendant No. 1 and 2 and requested them to not to raise the illegal construction on the said property but both the defendant No. 1 and 2 have not given any heed to the repeated requests of the plaintiff.

Therefore, the plaintiff has failed to prove his 'personal interest' in the subject matter and hence, the bar of section 41 (j) Specific Relief Act, 1963 is squarely applicable to the present case.
26. Moreover, the alleged unauthorized construction raised by the defendants was already complete when the present suit was filed.
There are no pleadings in regard to any threat or likelihood of a fresh construction in the suit property.
Therefore, in any event, there was no breach or attempt of breach of any obligation which would have warranted the suit for permanent injunction in the first place.
27. To summarize, the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit property and that his portion has suffered damage or his right to fresh air and light has been restricted.
Hence, the plaintiff is not entitled for any relief of injunction in respect of the suit property against the defendants.
Whether the suit of the plaintiff is barred by the provisions of Section 477/478 of the DMC Act for want of statutory notice? OPD-3 28.
It is the preliminary objection taken by defendant No.3/MCD that the suit is not maintainable as no statutory notice was served upon it in terms of section 478 of DMC Act, 1957.
Moreover, the basic object of sections 477 and 478 of DMC Act is to prevent matters from coming to court and once the matter has reached the court and is contested, the suit ought not be dismissed on technical grounds.
In this regard, reliance can be had to the judgment of Col. A. B. Singh (through LRs) v. Shri Chunnilal Sawhney and Others, 2011 SCC OnLine Del 4289.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Therefore, once defendant No.3/MCD has contested the present suit, it cannot be dismissed by recourse to section 477 and 478 of DMC Act.
Therefore, issue No.3 is decided against the defendant No.3 and in favour of the plaintiff.
Relief 29.
In view of my aforesaid findings, the suit of the plaintiff is dismissed.
Decree sheet be prepared accordingly.
No order as to costs.
